media.title: Reema Meets Ancient Numbers
media.context: Plays on M1.S1.T1.C2, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: On a pale parchment background, an old dusty book sits closed; it flips open and a slip of paper floats to the floor, covered in strange cuneiform symbols. A girl, Reema, picks it up; the caption 'What is this?' appears. The scene shifts to Reema running to her father, who smiles, while a simple map highlights Mesopotamia in western Asia (around present-day Iraq) with the caption 'Around 4000 years ago'. The cuneiform markings on the paper are shown beside the modern digits 7, 25, 100, 1000 written with the ten digits 0 through 9, with an arrow between the two sets of symbols. Four questions then appear one at a time on screen, 'Since when have humans been counting?', 'What was their need for counting? What were they counting?', 'How would the Mesopotamians have written 20? 50? 100?', and 'Since when have people been writing numbers in the modern form?', each holding on screen with a pause prompt. A closing card shows a notebook with the caption 'Jot down your best guess' before a fade.
media.teaching_notes: Play this at the very start of the chapter, before any teaching of number systems, to spark curiosity. First pause at about 22s on the floating mystery paper and ask students 'Would you still call these markings numbers? Why or why not?' before the father explains. The most important attempt-before-reveal moment is Scene 4 (85-130s): pause as each of the four questions appears, especially at about 115s on 'How would the Mesopotamians have written 20? 50? 100?', and have students write a guess for every question in their notebooks before resuming; do not let the video or your explanation answer them. Point to the side-by-side comparison at about 70s and ask 'Why do the cuneiform symbols look so different from our digits 0 through 9?' Keep all four guesses so the class can revisit them at the end of the chapter.
media.generation_prompt: [Duration]: 150 seconds, matching the video duration. [Style]: 2D animation, clean whiteboard/parchment style with step-by-step reveal; pure white or subtle parchment background; Lilly font for all handwritten-style captions. [Scene sequence]: Scene 1 Hook (0-25s): An old dusty book flips open and a slip of paper floats down, covered in strange cuneiform markings. On-screen text: 'Would you still call these numbers?' Pause at 22s: narrator asks 'What would you call these strange markings?' Scene 2 Context (25-55s): Reema runs to her father holding the paper; a simple map fades in highlighting Mesopotamia in western Asia. On-screen text: 'Around 4000 years ago, Mesopotamia'. Father smiles as caption reads 'This is one of the ways they wrote their numbers!' Scene 3 Compare (55-85s): Place the cuneiform symbols on the left in Orange and the modern digits '7 25 100 1000' on the right in Navy Blue, with the caption 'just ten digits, 0 through 9'. An arrow connects the two. On-screen text: 'Different civilisations invented very different-looking systems.' Scene 4 The four questions (85-130s): Reveal each question one at a time, holding several seconds each: 'Since when have humans been counting?', 'What was their need for counting? What were they counting?', 'How would the Mesopotamians have written 20? 50? 100?', 'Since when have people been writing numbers in the modern form?' Pause at 115s: narrator asks 'What would you guess for each one?' Do NOT reveal any answers. Scene 5 Recap and bridge (130-150s): A notebook appears with caption 'Jot down your best guess for each question.' Closing text: 'Travel back in time with Reema and her father.' [Narration style]: calm, instructional storytelling; use phrases like 'Notice how these symbols look nothing like our digits' and 'The key idea here is that the symbols we write are an invention.' [Music]: none or very subtle. [Visual elements]: use the 5-colour palette (Navy Blue, Orange, pale yellow, grey, white); the strange/new cuneiform symbols in Orange, the stable modern digits 0-9 in Navy Blue; arrows showing the comparison between the two systems; clean handwritten-style numerals and captions; pale yellow highlight on the Mesopotamia map region.

media.title: Comparing collections by one-to-one matching
media.context: This opens the number systems chapter with the most basic comparison of all: linking members of two collections one to one until a side runs out. The worked example pairs 6 red beads with 6 blue beads and asks which colour has more. The figure matches them and shows both sides running out together.

media.teaching_notes: Match the beads with a finger rather than counting them, since counting is what the chapter is about to build. Ask how you would compare two collections without knowing any numbers. Then use unequal collections and let the leftovers decide.

media.title: A number system as a fixed-order standard sequence
labels: the symbol you stop on names the number
media.context: A number system is a standard sequence kept in a fixed order, and counting means matching a collection to that sequence and reading off where you stop. The worked example uses the letters a to z in order and asks which letter names a collection of 5 objects. The figure matches the collection to the sequence.
media.description: A number system as a fixed-order standard sequence: a labelled figure illustrating the idea, drawn from the worked example 'Using the letters a to z in order as the standard sequence (a is 1, b is 2, and so on), which letter names a collection of 5 objects?'.

media.teaching_notes: Match the objects in order and stop deliberately on the fifth. Ask what would change if the alphabet were shuffled. Then ask which letter names a collection of 9.

media.title: Numeral System Sorter
media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Ganita Prakash Chapter 3 'A Story of Numbers' — the Mechanism of Counting, the shortcomings of non-positional systems, and the Hindu number system. Read where the systems stop being a list and become a comparison: the class has met several ways of writing a number and now has to say what separates them. It uses the book's own vocabulary — landmark numbers, base-n, place value system, placeholder — and never the word 'Arabic numerals'; NCERT names it the Hindu / Indian number system, credited to India, with zero as both a placeholder and a number in its own right.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's placement, the correct cell, and the written forms that explain it.
whatYouLearned: A system is positional when place decides value, and has a zero when a symbol holds an empty place
The two properties are independent, so four cells are needed and not two
Column arithmetic needs both properties, which is what makes one system easier than another
Changing the system changes the writing and never the quantity

overview.goal: The student classifies numeral systems by whether they are positional and whether they have a zero, and justifies which property makes arithmetic easier.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain sorting table with a two by two grid above it, the way a set of cards is laid out and grouped on a desk. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class cannot agree which way of writing a number makes long addition easiest, and the grid is asked to settle it on properties instead of on taste.
overview.concept: Numeral systems differ in two independent ways. A positional system lets a symbol's place decide its value, so the same symbol means different amounts in different columns. A system with a zero has a symbol that holds an empty place. Column arithmetic needs both, which is why some systems make long addition easy and others do not.
overview.purpose: The student classifies numeral systems by whether they are positional and whether they have a zero, and justifies which property makes arithmetic easier.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Grid fills the upper main panel, card table beneath, addition demo to the right on a wide frame and below the table on a 390 px frame. Every card keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not pre-place any card while a prediction is still open, and never draw a glyph the system's own rules would not produce. An invented glyph would make the comparison meaningless.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Column addition works by adding like places and carrying into the next, which needs the places to be fixed by position and needs a symbol for an empty place so the columns stay lined up. A tally has neither, so there is nothing to add in columns. Subtractive pair numerals fix value by symbol rather than by place, so a column has no meaning. The two properties are independent, which is why the grid has four cells and not two. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

scenes.subGoal: Compactness is not position, so a shorter numeral is not automatically an easier one to compute with.

Answer: No: compactness and position are different properties, and only position gives a column meaning

learnMode.summary: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the card set from its own systems, shows the question, then reveals the correct cells, the written forms and the answer together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A change of numeral system changes the writing and never the amount. Breaks: Reading a longer written form as a larger number. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): Position and a placeholder zero are independent properties, so a system can have one without the other. Breaks: Treating position and zero as a single package that a system either has or lacks. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): Compactness is not position, so a shorter numeral is not automatically an easier one to compute with. Breaks: Reading a compact written form as evidence that the system supports column arithmetic. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): The zero symbol only earns its place once position has already created the columns. Breaks: Zero seen only as nothing, so it is expected to appear in any system that counts. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): A justification has to name one of the two properties the grid is built on. Breaks: Believing all numeral systems work like ours, so familiarity is mistaken for a property.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the four cards face up with the grid EMPTY and the addition panel closed, and ask the class which system would make a long addition easiest. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Target the quantity every card is writing, read from the quantity readout. Never sort a card before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Send the cards into their cells one at a time and name the property that decided each one, pointing at the positional axis and then at the zero axis. Targets the two axes and the four cells. Say for each card which of the two questions it answered yes to, and read the cell counts from the tool's own readout. Call 3. Run the same addition in the sorted system and then in the system with neither property, and leave the failed attempt on screen. Targets the addition panel in the positional cell with a zero and then in the cell with neither property. Read every number in the working from the tool's own state, never from memory.

hunts: EMPTY CELL HUNT: try to find any system that is not positional and still has a zero, then say why the search fails.
SAME QUANTITY: set one quantity, expand all four cards, and find the card that uses the most symbols and the one that uses the fewest.
BROKEN COLUMNS: run the addition demo in a system that is not positional and describe exactly where the columns stop lining up.
PROPERTY OR PREFERENCE: write a reason one system is easier, then check whether it names position or the zero.

observationsAndConclusions.why: A cell is decided by two property answers, positional and has a zero, and by nothing else
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Two cards sit in different cells even though both are old ways of writing a number
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Systems are separated by what they can do, not by how old or how unfamiliar they look

observationsAndConclusions.why: A system can fix value by place and still have no symbol for an empty place, so the two properties do not arrive together
observationsAndConclusions.observe: One cell holds a system that is positional and still has no zero
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The zero was a separate invention, which is why the grid cannot be collapsed to two cells

observationsAndConclusions.why: Column addition adds like places and carries into the next, and in that system there are no places to be alike
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The addition demo piles symbols up with nothing to line up when the system is not positional
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Watching a method fail is the argument; the easier system is easier for a reason that can be named

media.description: Cards on a sorting table each write ONE quantity in a different numeral system, and every written form is GENERATED from that quantity by the system's own rules rather than stored as a picture — the tally in fives with the fifth stroke drawn diagonally across the four before it, the subtractive pair by the Class-6 landmark rules, the Brahmi card with a separate sign for each number and each ten, the repeated tens sign as a power sign repeated up to nine times, the base sixty card in sixty columns with an EMPTY column left blank, and the ten digit place value card one digit per column. A two by two grid above the table asks the cards two questions and only two: does the PLACE decide the value, and is there a symbol that holds an empty place open. A card dropped in the wrong cell is not marked with a cross; it travels back to the table and names the property it failed. Tapping a card opens it into one drawn glyph per symbol with a live count, so a subtractive pair like XLIV can be checked by pointing rather than by re-reading. An addition demo runs the same sum in whichever system is chosen, including the systems where it visibly fails: in the positional system with a zero the digits stand in columns and a carry travels left, and in the subtractive pair system the symbols pool with nothing to align and the failure is left on screen rather than cleared. A reason that says one system is easier because it is familiar is refused as a preference, and the student is asked which of the two properties it rests on.

concept.notation: The grid axes are positional or not positional, and has a zero or has no zero. A system's cell is decided by those two questions and by nothing else.
concept.statement: Numeral systems differ in two independent ways. A positional system lets a symbol's place decide its value, so the same symbol means different amounts in different columns. A system with a zero has a symbol that holds an empty place. Column arithmetic needs both, which is why some systems make long addition easy and others do not.
prerequisites: reading a quantity written in more than one way
misconceptions: Belief that all numeral systems work like ours, so position is assumed everywhere.
Zero seen only as nothing rather than as a placeholder that holds a column open.
concept.why_it_is_true: Column addition works by adding like places and carrying into the next, which needs the places to be fixed by position and needs a symbol for an empty place so the columns stay lined up. A tally has neither, so there is nothing to add in columns. Subtractive pair numerals fix value by symbol rather than by place, so a column has no meaning. The two properties are independent, which is why the grid has four cells and not two.
worked_numbers: Tally: not positional, no zero, so 27 is 27 separate marks and addition is recounting.
Subtractive pair: not positional, no zero, so XXVII carries its value in its symbols and column addition has nothing to line up.
Ten digit place value: positional with a zero, so 27 plus 45 is two column sums and one carry.

extra: Cutting one notch on a stick for every run scored in a gully cricket match
A shopkeeper's tally sheet where every fifth stroke is drawn across the four before it
The numerals on an old wall clock, where a symbol carries its own value wherever it sits

A lift panel where the label on a button and the height of the floor are two different things
A house number where the digits matter and the order of the digits matters more
A cash memo where the same amount is written once in digits and once in words

answer_key.worked: A system is positional when place decides value, and has a zero when a symbol holds an empty place. Column arithmetic needs both.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn cards: the correct cell for each card, the written form of a quantity in a named system, or whether a stated reason cites position or zero.
answer_key.precision: Every written form is generated from the quantity by the system's own rules, never stored as a picture, so a card cannot show a form its system would not produce.
answer_key.ground_truth: properties(system) = {positional: boolean, hasZero: boolean}, held as data. cell(system) = the grid cell those two booleans name. writtenForm(quantity, system) = generated by the system's rules. reasonValid(text) = whether the reason cites position or zero rather than preference.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.case: A system that is positional but has no zero
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: It occupies its own cell and the tool keeps it there. The base sixty system is exactly this case, and collapsing the grid to two cells would hide why zero was a separate invention.

edge_cases.case: A card dropped in a cell it does not belong to
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: It returns to the table with the property it failed named, rather than being marked wrong. The property is the reason.

edge_cases.case: A reason that says one system is easier because it is familiar
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Rejected as a preference rather than a property. The tool asks which of position or zero the reason rests on.

edge_cases.case: The same quantity across all four cards
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The quantity never changes when the card changes, and the tool says so, because the point is that the writing differs and the number does not.

edge_cases.case: An addition demo in a non positional system
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The demo runs and visibly fails to line up columns, rather than being disabled. Watching it not work is the argument.

practice.shows: The item's own cards, the question, the answer affordance, a running score, and the Finish button.
steps: One item at a time from props.questions; the tool never re-orders or filters the bank.
practice.review: The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's placement, the correct cell, and the written forms that explain it.
practice.done_when: The bank is exhausted (emit bank_done, not terminal) or the student presses Finish (emit finished, once).
practice.opens_with: Item 1 of the bank, cards on the table, grid empty, score at 0.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example running the addition in a system a child champions and letting the columns settle it.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

steps: In that system a mark's value depends on which sixty column it sits in, so it is positional.

steps: A zero is the symbol that holds a column open when nothing is in it.
In a system that is not positional there are no columns to hold open.
So a zero would have no job to do, and no system invents a symbol with no job.
That is why the fourth cell stays empty while the other three fill.
items.answer: A zero has nothing to hold open without columns, so that cell has no members

steps: The grid sorts cards by two questions only: is it positional, and does it have a zero.
Being familiar is not either of those questions.
The addition demo lines up into columns for a positional system with a zero and for no other card.
So the reason must rest on position or on the zero, not on habit.
items.answer: No: familiarity is a preference, and the grid only accepts position or the zero as a reason

visual_behaviour.never: Do not pre-place any card while a prediction is still open, and never draw a glyph the system's own rules would not produce. An invented glyph would make the comparison meaningless.
visual_behaviour.scene: A two by two grid labelled on both axes, with numeral system cards on a table beneath. Each card carries its system name and the quantity written in that system as inline SVG glyphs. An expanded card opens to show the writing rules; the addition demo runs in a panel beside the grid.
visual_behaviour.layout: Grid fills the upper main panel, card table beneath, addition demo to the right on a wide frame and below the table on a 390 px frame. Every card keeps a 44 px hit target.
readouts: The quantity every card is writing, always on screen
How many cards sit in each cell, live
For the expanded card: whether it is positional and whether it has a zero
animations: Card lock: a correct placement settles into its cell over 160 ms and both axis labels brighten, so the two properties are seen to be what decided it.
Card return: a wrong placement travels back over 220 ms and opens on arrival to show the property it fails.

Addition demo: in a positional system the digits slide into columns and a carry travels left; in a non positional one the symbols pile up with nothing to align, and the failure is left on screen rather than cleared.
visual_behaviour.scale_rule: Card size is derived from the panel width and the card count so every glyph stays at least 16 px; the table scrolls horizontally rather than shrinking cards below a 44 px hit target.

teaching_sequence.rationale: The cards have to be seen separating along two independent axes before positional and has a zero are named, or the two properties collapse into one vague feeling that some systems are modern and others are not

tool_config.image_prompts_note: Empty by design. This mount is a mechanism, not a depiction, and the standard mandates hand-built inline SVG with no external asset dependency, so no depictive picture is declared.
mathematical_facts: A system is positional when the place of a symbol decides its value
A system has a zero when one of its symbols holds an empty place open
The two properties are independent, which is why the grid has four cells and not two
Column addition needs both properties, so a system with neither has nothing to line up

question_integration.test: Freeze any injected step and ask: could the teacher read every number in this question off THIS screen? If not, fix the scene, not the words.
question_integration.parse_rule: Read the systems out of the question text and lay a card for each. Read the quantity the question names and generate every card's written form from it. When the question names a target cell, load it without revealing which cards belong there.
question_integration.compute_rule: Build the scene from the parsed numbers, then compute the answer with the tool's own ground truth function ON THE DRAWN SCENE. Never carry the bank's answer as truth while drawing a different scene. The two must agree by construction; if they disagree the scene is wrong, not the bank.

question_integration.sceneless_rule: A general claim with no systems in it ('why does column addition need a zero?') has nothing to sort. Render an authored, self consistent case that exhibits the claim, in this tool the same sum worked in ten digit place value and in subtractive pair side by side, one in columns and one not, rather than fabricating a scene the question does not describe.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to separate the WRITING from the NUMBER before either property is named. Four cards, one quantity, and the readout says 27 under every one of them while the tally card runs to twenty-seven marks and the digit card to two. Sweep the quantity in Free Play afterwards if the class needs it: the length changes and the number never does. Do not name 'positional' at this beat — the cards have to be seen separating before the property is given a word.

Beat 2 is the whole argument in one motion. Five cards fall into the grid on two questions, and the base sixty card lands in a cell of its own — positional, and still no zero. That single card is why the grid has four cells and not two, and why zero reads as a SEPARATE invention rather than as part of a package. The fourth cell, not positional and has a zero, stays visibly empty: a placeholder has no job where there are no columns to hold open.

Beat 3 turns the observation into a test. The same sum, 47 + 85, is worked twice: in the ten digit place value system it lands in two column sums with two carries, and in the subtractive pair system the ten symbols of XLVII and LXXXV pool with nothing to line up, and that failure is LEFT on the screen. Read the carry count and the pooled count off the tool, never from memory. The point to say out loud is that the easier system is easier for a reason that can be named.
media.generation_prompt: Numeral System Sorter: cards showing one quantity in tally, subtractive pair, Brahmi and ten digit place value sorted into a two by two grid of positional or not and has a zero or not
media.instructions_for_student: Ask each card two questions and only two. Does the PLACE a symbol sits in decide its value? Is there a symbol that holds an empty place open? Those two answers name the card's cell — nothing else does, and how old or how familiar a system looks is not one of the questions. Open a card to see the quantity written out one symbol at a time, and count the symbols by pointing at them. Then run the addition in a system and watch what happens: where the places are fixed and an empty place can be held open, the digits stand in columns and a carry moves left; where they are not, the symbols simply pile up with nothing to line up under anything.

media.title: Two Flocks and No Numbers
media.context: This hook opens the topic on one to one matching and on a standard sequence. Students have no formal counting theory. The film must not describe what a counting system needs and must not name the technique.
media.description: Two shepherds meet at a river, each with a flock, and neither can count past three. They line the animals up nose to nose, one of yours against one of mine, until one side runs out, and the leftovers say exactly by how many.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Compare two collections by one to one matching, and say what a counting system must provide. Key teaching points: 1) Matching one against one compares two collections exactly. 2) The leftovers give the difference without any counting. 3) The method becomes impractical for very large collections. 4) A counting system needs a fixed sequence of names that never runs out. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often think comparison requires counting both collections first. 2) Students often assume any list of names would serve as a counting system. Pause points: 0:23, at the end of the leftovers answer: ask how the shepherds knew the difference. 0:23, just before the open question: ask what would go wrong with a thousand animals each. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask whether you need numbers to compare two piles. After viewing, ask what a good sequence of number names must do.

  RENDERER

    what the leftovers say: exactly by how many

    Total running time 35 seconds across 3 scenes.

    Scene 1. Nose to nose
      Duration: 12 seconds.
      On screen at the start: an empty dark slate frame.
      Beats:

      Duration: 11 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s1_caption.
      Beats:

      Narration: "They line the animals up nose to nose, one of yours against one of mine, again and again, until one side finally runs out. Whoever has animals left over wins."

media.title: Stone Age Questions and Method 1, Counting with Sticks
media.context: Plays on M1.S2.T2.C13, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: The video opens on a Stone Age scene set ten thousand years ago, with a herd of cows beside a hut and on-screen text 'How would you check that none of your cows has gone missing?'. It animates the three natural questions Q1, Q2 and Q3 appearing one at a time on parchment. Next it draws a one-to-one mapping: for every cow, a single stick is placed, with an arrow linking each cow to its own stick and the caption 'one-to-one mapping'. A growing table is revealed showing 1 as |, 2 as ||, 3 as |||, 4 as ||||, 5 as |||||. The scene then shows Nani near Indore dropping one white pebble into a clay pot for each of twelve goats, then removing one pebble per goat that returns, with the caption 'If any pebbles remain, a goat is missing'. Finally it animates two piles of sticks being paired one from each pile, with leftover sticks highlighted in Orange, and poses the CHECK question on-screen without revealing the answer.
media.teaching_notes: Play this before students attempt the CHECK task, as the introduction to Method 1 of counting. First pause at about 22s on the Hook ('How would you check that none of your cows has gone missing?') and ask students to predict, in pairs, what object they would use before sticks are revealed, this is the attempt-before-reveal moment, so let them propose ideas before Scene 3 plays. Pause again at about 90s on the stick table (1 |, 2 ||, ... 5 |||||) and point to how each new number simply adds one more stick, asking 'Why does each row gain exactly one stick?'. At the final CHECK screen near 150s, stop the video and ask the predict-the-next-step question 'After pairing the two piles, what would the leftover sticks tell you about Q2 and Q3?' and have students write their reasoning in their notebooks before any class discussion, do not reveal the answer, since working it out is the whole point of this topic.

media.title: Counting with Body Parts, The Papua New Guinea System
media.context: Plays on M1.S2.T2.C14, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: On a parchment background, the video opens with the question "What if your counting system was always with you, ON you?" Scene two draws a single human figure and labels body parts in order, animating a glowing path: fingers of one hand, then wrist, elbow, shoulder, neck, ear, eye, top of head, then mirroring the same locations on the opposite side until 27 distinct locations are numbered 1 through 27. Scene three follows a boy counting eight friends: an Orange marker hops finger-1, finger-2, finger-3, finger-4, finger-5, then wrist (6), forearm (7), elbow (8), with the caption "elbow = 8". A panel then shows three equivalent representations side by side, Tally ||||||||, Roman VIII, and Body-part "elbow". The final scene poses the on-screen CHECK question "If he has ten friends, which body part does he stop at?" and pauses with the sequence finger, wrist, elbow, shoulder partly traced.
media.teaching_notes: When to play: use after students have met one-to-one counting in Method 1, as a concept-introduction before they attempt the CHECK question themselves; it can also anchor a review of "different number systems for the same quantity". Pause at about 95s (right after wrist 6 and forearm 7, before elbow 8 is revealed): point to the Orange marker on the forearm and ask "Predict, which body part comes next, and what count will it name?" Let students answer before resuming so the elbow = 8 reveal confirms their prediction. Pause again at about 137s on the final CHECK screen "If the boy has ten friends, which body part does he stop at?": do NOT play past the traced finger, wrist, elbow, shoulder, have students trace the fixed sequence on paper or on their own arm and commit to an answer. Ask "Why does this stay accurate even without digits?" to surface that the order is fixed and the final location named is the count, and "Why can't this system count past 27?"

media.title: Method 3, Written Symbols, Numerals, and the Idea of a Number System
media.context: Plays on M1.S2.T2.C15, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: The video opens on a parchment background with a pile of sticks overflowing past the edge and a row of letters fading out, captioned "Sticks run out of room. Letters run out of letters." A title card slides in: "Method 3, Written Symbols". Table 1 is then drawn row by row in a clean handwritten style, with the Number row in grey and the Rep. row beneath it: I, II, III, IV, V, VI, VII, VIII, IX, X, then XI through XX. As each cell appears, one extra stroke is animated onto the previous numeral, and the anchor symbols V and X are highlighted in Orange while I stays Navy Blue. Worked-example overlays flash "7 = VII", "13 = XIII", "20 = XX". A pause card poses the textbook prompt about extending the method to bigger numbers. A final split-screen shows "XII" and "12" joined by an arrow to the caption "the same number, twelve", separating numeral from number, then a closing recap of sticks, names, and written symbols.
media.teaching_notes: Play this AFTER students have seen Method 1 (sticks) and Method 2 (letter sounds) but BEFORE the formal Roman numerals topic, as a bridge into written symbols. Pause at 95-100s on the frozen Table 1 and the on-screen prompt "Do you see a way of extending this method to represent bigger numbers?", this is the attempt-before-reveal moment: have every student write at least one idea in their notebook before you resume, and do not let the class call out an answer. Pause again at about 60s, point to the column where IV and V sit, and ask "Why did the system introduce V instead of just writing IIIII?" to surface the anchor-symbol idea. As a "predict the next step" check, pause just before XX is drawn (around 90s) and ask "What comes after XIX, predict the numeral before it appears." End by pointing at the XII / 12 split-screen and asking students to state in their own words the difference between a number and a numeral.

media.title: Method 2, Using Letter Sounds as Number Names
media.context: Plays on M1.S2.T2.C16, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: The video opens on a parchment background with a pile of sticks beside a herd, a bag of grain, and a village of people, captioned 'Can we count without carrying anything at all?' as the sticks fade out. A recall card slides in showing one-to-one mapping between sticks and objects from Method 1, then transforms into the title 'Method 2, Using Letter Sounds'. The English letters 'a' to 'z' animate in order along a line, and a clean table is drawn pairing Number with its representation: 1-a, 2-b, 3-c, 4-d, then dots, then 26-z. A shopkeeper scene animates four saris on a shelf; a finger touches each sari in turn while the letters 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd' pop up one per sari, and the caption 'The final letter names the count' highlights 'd' in Orange. An error-alert card notes the letter is just a label for a position in a fixed ordered sequence. Finally the alphabet line runs to 'z' and stops with the caption 'After z, we run out of letters', then a Math Talk question card appears and the screen holds on the pause prompt.

content.text: To compare two collections, link one member of each collection together, over and over, until one side runs out. This is called a one-to-one matching. If both sides run out at the same time, the collections are equal. If one side still has objects left over, that side is larger, and the number left over tells you exactly how many more the smaller side needs to catch up. You can do all of this without knowing any number names at all.

content.text: A number system is just a standard sequence of objects, names, or symbols kept in a fixed order. To count a collection, you match its members to this sequence in order; the symbol you stop on is the number's name. Sticks give an unending sequence, so they never run out, but they get clumsy for big counts. The letters a to z are easy to say but there are only 26 of them, so they cannot name a collection bigger than 26. A good number system must never run out of symbols.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what pairing the members of two collections one to one reveals through observation and reasoning, and determine that when both sides run out together the collections are equal, while any objects left over mark the larger side and count exactly how many more the smaller side needs. They will explain that this comparison names which collection is bigger and by how much without any counting words or digits at all.

Students will be able to infer what a fixed-order standard sequence does for counting through observation and reasoning, and determine that the symbol a count stops on is its name, so a sequence of only twenty-six letters can name no collection larger than twenty-six. They will explain that a usable number system must be an unending sequence, since a finite set of symbols eventually runs out and leaves large collections with no name.

media.title: Grouping tally marks into a fixed size
labels: bundling does not change the count
media.context: A long row of single tally marks is hard to read, so the marks are bundled into equal groups and the count is read as the group size times the number of groups, plus what is left. The worked example bundles 23 tally marks into groups of 5. The figure bundles and reads the total.

media.title: The Big Idea, Counting in Groups and the Perceptual Limit
media.context: Plays on M2.S3.T3.C21, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: The video opens on three separate continents lighting up on a parchment world map, each marked with a small group of people, while the caption 'Count by grouping' appears. A pair of dots animates over and over to show counting in 2s for the Gumulgal, then group-size badges reading '2, 5, 10, 20' slide in along a row. Small boxes are then drawn one at a time, each filling with objects, chickens, flowers, nesting dolls, logs, a dog, a bunch of grapes, berries, sticks, and a pyramid, under the on-screen question 'Up to what group size could you immediately see the number of objects without counting?'. A box of 5-or-more objects flashes and a caption notes most people cannot read it at a glance. Tally marks are drawn and every group of 5 is swept up and replaced by a new symbol. A Diwali scene draws diyas along a boundary wall in rows of ten, revealing 'thirty-two' after three rows plus two. The final scene posts the two CHECK prompts and a 'next: Roman numerals' bridge card.
media.teaching_notes: Play this AFTER students have tried the Gumulgal counting-in-2s idea but BEFORE Roman numerals. First pause at about 80s, on the boxes-in-a-box activity question 'Up to what group size could you immediately see the number of objects without counting?', stop here as an attempt-before-reveal moment and have each student write down their own glance limit in their notebook before the video shows the perceptual limit. Resume, then pause again at about 105s on the five-tally-marks-to-one-symbol transformation and point to the arrow, asking 'Why does replacing every five marks with one symbol make the number easier to read?'. At the closing CHECK prompts (around 150s) freeze the frame: do NOT let students call out answers, instead ask them to predict 'How would you represent 1345 using only groups of 5?' and 'What goes wrong if you only ever use one group size?' and collect attempts before moving to the Roman-numerals topic. Reinforce the ERROR ALERT verbally: the group size is a human choice, not always 10.

media.title: Tally Marks on Bones, Ishango and Lebombo
media.context: Plays on M2.S3.T3.C22, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: The video opens on a parchment-style surface with the on-screen question 'What surface would you scratch a count on, forty-four thousand years ago?' as a hand sketches a bone. It then animates the mark-for-each-object rule: single vertical strokes appear one by one, then groups of five are bound with a diagonal line like ||||. A daily-life scene draws a Surat cloth-shop owner making one stroke per silk sari roll, revealing four full groups of five and three extra strokes captioned 'twenty-three rolls'. Two artefacts are then drawn side by side with captions: the Ishango bone (20,000 to 35,000 years old, columns of notches) in Orange, and the Lebombo bone (44,000 years old, 29 notches) in Navy Blue, with an arrow labelled 'one notch per object'. The final scene poses the CHECK question on-screen and holds without answering it.
media.teaching_notes: Play this when introducing tally marks, ideally right after students have met Method 1 (one stick per object) and the Papua New Guinea body-part system, so the connection lands. Pause at about 0:90 (the Surat sari-roll example) and point to the four groups of five plus three extra strokes, then ask students to predict: 'If he sees one more roll, what tally would he draw, and what is the new total?' before resuming. Pause again at the final scene (about 2:10) on the CHECK question; do NOT let the video answer it, point to the 29 notches on the Lebombo bone and ask 'Why could the same 29 notches mean a count of cattle OR a lunar calendar, what do both interpretations share about the number 29?' Use this as an attempt-before-reveal: have students write one sentence on their own before you discuss. Optionally pause at the two-bones scene (about 1:50) and ask 'Which bone is older, and how do you know from the captions?'

It then animates the mark-for-each-object rule: single vertical strokes appear one by one, then groups of five are bound with a diagonal line like ||||. A daily-life scene draws a Surat cloth-shop owner making one stroke per silk sari roll, revealing four full groups of five and three extra strokes captioned 'twenty-three rolls'. Two artefacts are then drawn side by side with captions: the Ishango bone (20,000 to 35,000 years old, columns of notches) in Orange, and the Lebombo bone (44,000 years old, 29 notches) in Navy Blue, with an arrow labelled 'one notch per object'. The final scene poses the CHECK question on-screen and holds without answering it.

media.title: Counting in Twos, The Gumulgal System
media.context: Plays on M2.S3.T3.C27, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: The video opens on a parchment scroll posing the question: a number system with words for only six numbers, where anything bigger is "too many", appearing on three different continents. A world map highlights Australia, South America, and South Africa with glowing pins. The Gumulgal word list animates in line by line, urapon (1), ukasar (2), ukasar-urapon (3), ukasar-ukasar (4), ukasar-ukasar-urapon (5), ukasar-ukasar-ukasar (6), and an on-screen caption asks the viewer to read them aloud and spot the pattern. Orange brackets then group each name into 2s and 1s, with arrows revealing 3 = 2 + 1, 4 = 2 + 2, 5 = 2 + 2 + 1, 6 = 2 + 2 + 2, and the label ras for any number greater than 6. A worked example writes 5 = 2 + 2 + 1 and swaps each 2 for 'ukasar' and each 1 for 'urapon'. The closing scene places the Gumulgal, Bakairi, and Bushmen word lists side by side and poses the common-ancestor question.
media.teaching_notes: Play this when introducing the Gumulgal system, ideally before students have seen the pattern stated, so they can discover it. Pause at 50s on the six Gumulgal names (point to the repeating 'ukasar' in each line) and let students attempt the pattern themselves before the reveal at 55s, ask "How is the name for 3 built from the names for 2 and 1?" and "Can you see how the other names are formed?" before resuming. This is the attempt-before-reveal pause. Pause again at 125s where '7 = 2 + 2 + 2 + 1' is shown and have students complete Step 2 in their notebooks (translate each term using 'ukasar' for 2 and 'urapon' for 1) before any continuation. Finally, pause on the closing screen (around 158s) and ask "Is the common-ancestor theory the only explanation, or could three groups independently discover the same idea?", collect alternatives without confirming a 'correct' one, since the next topic pursues this.

media.context: Plays on M2.S3.T3.C32, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: The video opens on a wall clock with I, II, III, IV ... XII around its face, then a caption appears: 'I = 1, V = 5, X = 10'. A parchment panel lists the rule 'Group into 10s, then 5s, then 1s'. Scene by scene it animates the number 27: two X symbols slide in for 10 + 10, one V slides in for 5, then two I symbols for 1 + 1, building XXVII while the running line '27 = 10 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1' is written underneath. An Orange arrow highlights the largest-symbol-first order. A new landmark table is drawn in, I V X L C D M with 1 5 10 50 100 500 1,000, and IV / XL are shown as 'one less' with a subtract arrow. The faded Example 2 poses 'Write 14' and freezes at 'What do you write for 4?'. A final card shows the CHECK prompt 'Convert 38 using the additive rule only'.

Pause again at 140s on 'Step 3: What do you write for 4?' (the faded Example 2) and have students write their answer for 4 in their notebooks before revealing, this is the attempt-before-reveal moment; point to the subtract arrow and ask 'Why is the smaller symbol placed before the larger one here?' At the final CHECK card, stop the video and assign 'Convert 38 using the additive rule only' as independent work; do not let the video reveal XXXVIII first. Point to the landmark table at 95s when discussing why 50 gets its own symbol L instead of XXXXX.

media.title: Roman Numeral Arithmetic Challenges
media.context: Plays on M2.S3.T3.C33, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: The video opens on a parchment surface with the caption 'Add CCXXXII + CCCXIII, no modern digits allowed' and a spinning question mark. A small landmark-value table fades in: I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100, D = 500, M = 1000. The two Roman numerals CCXXXII and CCCXIII are written one above the other, then the symbols are sorted into separate columns of Cs, Xs, and Is, showing 5 Cs + 4 Xs + 5 Is. Arrows animate each bundling: 5 Cs collapse into one D, then 5 Is collapse into one V, and 4 Xs are rewritten as XL. The pieces D, XL, V slide together largest-first to form DCXLV, and a check line writes 232 + 313 = 545 and D (500) + XL (40) + V (5) = 545 with a tick. A faded panel shows 'Do it yourself: LXXXVII + LXXVIII' and the screen holds. A final caption lists V × L, L × D, V × D, VII × IX under 'Multiplication is even worse' and bridges to place value and the digit 0.
media.teaching_notes: Play this AFTER students have attempted the HOOK problem on their own (add CCXXXII + CCCXIII with no modern digits) so they have already felt the difficulty before the method appears. First pause at 22s on 'What would you group first?', point to the two stacked numerals and ask students to predict whether they would start from the Is or the Cs, and why starting largest-first helps. Attempt-before-reveal pause at 140s on 'Do it yourself: LXXXVII + LXXVIII', stop the video here, point to the faded panel, and have every student bundle the Ls, Xs, Vs, and Is in their notebook and write a final Roman numeral before you resume. After the check at ~115s, ask 'Why did we get a tick, what makes DCXLV equal to 545?' and then 'Why is the C-to-D pairing 5x but D-to-M only 2x, and how does that inconsistency make multiplication harder?' Use the closing V × L, L × D, V × D, VII × IX line as a discussion springboard, not a worked answer.

media.title: Roman Numerals, Representing Large Numbers with Landmark Numbers
media.context: Plays on M2.S3.T3.C34, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: On a parchment background, the number 2367 appears, then breaks apart into its landmark sum 1000 + 1000 + 100 + 100 + 100 + 50 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1, each piece tagged with its symbol M, C, L, X, V, I and animated into the numeral MMCCCLXII. A caption reads "Largest landmark first". The seven landmark symbols I (1), V (5), X (10), L (50), C (100), D (500), M (1000) line up in a decreasing-value row with arrows. Worked Example 1 builds 1222 = M C C X X I I → MCCXXII step by step. Worked Example 2 shows 2999 decomposed largest-first and pauses with "Step 2 (you complete)". A "Figure it Out" panel lists 1222, 2999, 302, 715 and holds. A side note shows the subtractive shortcut MMCMXCIX next to the additive form, and an ERROR ALERT crosses out the wrong "MMM minus one" idea. The closing card recaps that grouping by a sequence of landmark numbers is the breakthrough.
media.teaching_notes: Play this after students have met the seven landmark symbols (Topic 10/11) and tried at least one small Roman numeral on their own, so the scaling-up to four-digit numbers lands as an extension rather than a first exposure. First pause at 50s on the 2367 decomposition: point to the row '1000 + 1000 + 100 + 100 + 100 ...' and ask the class to predict the next symbol after the three Cs before the video plays L, an attempt-before-reveal moment. Second pause at 110s on Worked Example 2 ('Step 2 you complete'): freeze the frame and have every student write the full numeral for 2999 in additive style on paper before un-pausing; then ask 'Why must the symbols be written in decreasing value order?' Hold the 'Figure it Out' panel at ~125s and assign (iii) 302 and (iv) 715 as the in-class task, do NOT let the video reveal these; the video deliberately leaves them unanswered. Close by asking the CHECK question aloud: 'Why does the Roman system need seven symbols instead of one or two?'

topics.summary: Humans invented grouping and landmark numbers so a big count becomes readable. Marks bundled into fives, names counted in twos, and Roman landmark symbols all beat a plain tally.

content.text: A tally puts one mark for each object, but a big pile of single marks is hard to read. If you bundle the marks into equal groups of a fixed size, say five, you can read the count as the group size times the number of full groups, plus the few marks left over. For example, 4 groups of five and 3 over is 5 times 4 plus 3, which is 23. Reading a grouped tally is much faster than counting single marks, which is exactly why people started grouping.

content.text: Some peoples counted in groups of two. Using urapon for one and ukasar for a pair, every number is written as a string of ukasar, one for each pair, and a single urapon at the end if the number is odd. So 5 is ukasar-ukasar-urapon, which is 2 plus 2 plus 1, and 8 is four ukasar. To read a name, count 2 for every ukasar and 1 for every urapon and add them up. Counting in a fixed group size like two is already shorter to write than a plain tally.

content.text: The Roman system gives a new symbol to certain landmark numbers: I is 1, V is 5, X is 10, L is 50, C is 100, D is 500, M is 1000. To write a number, break it into these landmarks from the largest downward and write the symbols in that order. A smaller symbol before a larger one means one landmark less, so 4 is IV and 9 is IX and 40 is XL. To read a numeral, add the symbols, subtracting whenever a smaller one sits before a larger one. Landmark numbers let a few symbols stand for large numbers, far more compactly than a tally.

For example, 4 groups of five and 3 over is 5 times 4 plus 3, which is 23. Reading a grouped tally is much faster than counting single marks, which is exactly why people started grouping. Some peoples counted in groups of two. Using urapon for one and ukasar for a pair, every number is written as a string of ukasar, one for each pair, and a single urapon at the end if the number is odd. So 5 is ukasar-ukasar-urapon, which is 2 plus 2 plus 1, and 8 is four ukasar. To read a name, count 2 for every ukasar and 1 for every urapon and add them up. learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what bundling single tally marks into equal groups achieves through observation and reasoning, and determine that the total is the group size times the number of full bundles plus the leftover marks, so four groups of five and three over is twenty-three. They will explain that a grouped tally is read far faster than one plain mark per object, which is exactly why people began bundling their marks.

Students will be able to infer what a system built on pairs records through observation and reasoning, and determine that each pair-word stands for two and a single unit-word for a leftover one, so a string of three pair-words with one unit is seven. They will explain that reading such a name means counting two for every pair-word and one for the leftover, and that grouping in twos is already shorter to write than a plain tally.

Students will be able to infer what a set of landmark symbols does for writing numbers through observation and reasoning, and determine that a number is built by taking landmarks from largest to smallest, with a smaller symbol before a larger one meaning one landmark less, so four is IV and ninety is XC. They will explain that reading adds the symbols while subtracting whenever a smaller one sits before a larger one, letting a few landmarks stand for large numbers far more compactly than a tally.

media.title: The Egyptian Number System, Base-10 Landmark Numbers
media.context: Plays on M3.S4.T4.C45, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: The video opens on a parchment background with the on-screen question 'The Romans had seven landmark symbols. The Egyptians had eight. Why is that such a big deal?' It then animates pebbles being grouped: one pebble (1), then ten collections grouping into 10, then ten tens grouping into 100, with each landmark number captioned and a label 'Each landmark number is 10 times the previous one.' The eight hieroglyph symbols are drawn one by one beneath their values 1, 10, 10², 10³, 10⁴, 10⁵, 10⁶, 10⁷ (| ∩ 9 𝖠⁺ 𝒞 finger, astonished man, sun). A worked example animates 324 = 100 + 100 + 100 + 10 + 10 + 4 decomposing into 999∩∩||||. A faded panel shows 1023 = 1000 + 10 + 10 + 3 and pauses on the 'Figure it Out' prompt without revealing the answer. The closing frame recaps 'how many hundreds? how many tens? how many ones?' and bridges to place value.
media.teaching_notes: Play this after students have met Roman landmark numbers and before they attempt the 'Figure it Out' practice prompts, so the pebble-grouping rule is fresh when they write their own numerals. Pause at 50s on the pebble grouping and ask students to predict the next landmark number after 100 before the symbols scene reveals it. Pause again at 138s on the faded 1023 panel and the 'Figure it Out' prompt, this is the attempt-before-reveal moment: have students complete 1023 in hieroglyphs and decide the largest power of 10 that fits 10,458 on paper before resuming, since the video deliberately does not give the answer. During review, point to the 999∩∩|||| frame at around 120s and ask 'why did we start with the hundreds first and not the ones?' to connect the greedy largest-first rule to place value.

media.title: The Concept of Base, Generalising to Base-5 and Base-n
media.context: Plays on M3.S4.T4.C46, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: On a parchment background, the title "The Idea of a Base" appears beside the question "What if we grouped in fives instead?" The Egyptian landmark numbers 1, 10, 10², 10³ are shown, then the 10 is animated as it is replaced by a 5. A vertical ladder builds the base-5 landmark numbers one rung at a time: 5⁰ = 1, 5¹ = 5, 5² = 25, 5³ = 125, 5⁴ = 625, 5⁵ = 3125, each tagged with its symbol, triangle (△), square (□), hexagon, circle (○), wave, arrow. A worked example expresses 143 as 125 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 1, drawing one circle, three squares, and three triangles to give ○□□□△△△. The formal definition card states the first landmark number is 1 and every next is the current one multiplied by a fixed number n. A faded card poses "Express 50 in the base-5 system" and the "Figure it Out" prompt about base-7 and base-n landmark numbers, then holds on a pause screen.
media.teaching_notes: Play this after students have met the Egyptian base-10 system, as the bridge into base-n. First attempt-before-reveal pause at 92s on the base-5 ladder ('5⁰ ... 5⁵'): pause and ask students to predict the next landmark number before the arrow rung appears, point to the rung labels and the ×5 jump between them so they see each is 5 times the previous. Pause again at 130s, right after '143 = 125 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 1' resolves to ○□□□△△△, and ask 'Why did we subtract out 125 first instead of a smaller landmark?' to surface the largest-landmark-first rule. At the closing pause (around 150s) hold on the 'Express 50 in base-5' and the 'Figure it Out: landmark numbers of a base-n system' prompts and let students work them on paper before you reveal anything, do not play past the pause until they have attempted both.

media.title: Why Base Systems Shine, Addition in Egyptian Numerals
media.context: Plays on M3.S4.T4.C47, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: The video opens on a parchment surface with two Egyptian numerals to be added, each made of ∩ (tens) and | (ones) hieroglyphs, with a large "+" between them and the question "What does a base buy us when we add?" written above. Scene by scene, the symbols slide together as the caption "Step 1, Separate the two symbols" appears and a counter tallies "15 ∩ and 15 |". Next, ten | strokes glow in Orange, collapse, and an arrow morphs them into one extra ∩ under "Step 2, Regroup the ones" (Is become 5, ∩s become 16). Then ten ∩ symbols animate into a single 𝟂 (hundred) coil under "Step 3, Regroup the tens" (∩s become 6, one 𝟂 appears). The final scene assembles "Sum = 𝟂 ∩∩∩∩∩∩ |||||" beside the column sum 132 + 33 = 165 and the words "10 of any landmark = 1 of the next landmark," then poses a "Figure it Out" prompt on screen.
media.teaching_notes: Play this AFTER students have attempted adding the two Egyptian numerals on their own, then use it to check their regrouping. Pause at 45s on "Total: 15 ∩ and 15 |" and ask students to predict: "Which landmark will we have to regroup first, and why can't we just write 15?" (point to the 15 | tally, connect to the Error Alert that no digit 15 exists). Attempt-before-reveal pause at 95s on "Step 3, Regroup the tens": stop before the hundred coil appears and ask "We have 16 ∩, what would you do next?" letting students answer before resuming. Finally, freeze on the closing "Figure it Out" card and have students work both addition problems in their notebooks; do NOT advance, since the video deliberately leaves it unsolved. Close by asking the CHECK question: "Why does Egyptian regrouping look like the carry rule? Answer in one sentence using the word base-10."

media.title: The Abacus and the Shortcomings of the Egyptian System
media.context: Plays on M3.S4.T4.C48, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: On a parchment-style board, the video opens with a medieval European scribe stuck writing numbers in Roman numerals, then reveals a board with horizontal lines labelled as a caption appears: 'The abacus: a base-10 calculator'. Starting from the line for 1, each successive line lights up to stand for a successive power of 10, drawn as clean handwritten counters. The number 3426 is grouped into powers of 10 on screen, then counters are placed line by line, 3 on the thousands line, 4 on the hundreds, 2 on the tens, and on the ones line 5 counters merge into 1 counter ABOVE the line worth 5, plus 1 counter on the line, while a caption reads 'above-the-line counter = 5'. A second board shows 2907 and 43 on either side of a vertical partition, counters pool together, and 7 ones + 3 ones combine into 10 ones with an arrow carrying 1 counter up to the tens line, then the screen freezes on the carry-rule question. The closing scene shows Egyptian symbols multiplying endlessly for higher powers of 10, with a caption 'an unending sequence of symbols', and poses the Figure-it-Out prompts.
media.teaching_notes: Play this AFTER students have grouped numbers into powers of 10 in the previous topic, and BEFORE they attempt the Figure-it-Out prompts on their own. First attempt-before-reveal pause at 122s on the caption 'Step 4: What is to be done if the total in a line exceeds 10?', pause here and have students predict the full carry sequence for 2907 + 43 and write the final answer in their notebooks before resuming; point to the Orange carry arrow when you restart. Second pause at 88s, point to the single counter sitting above the ones line and ask 'Why does that one counter stand for 5, not 1?' to check the above-the-line rule. At the closing scene (130-165s) freeze on the three Figure-it-Out prompts and do NOT let the video or yourself reveal answers, ask 'Why can no Egyptian symbol appear 10 or more times?' and have students justify it using the regrouping rule. Ask the predict-the-next-step question 'What carries to the next line, and what gets left behind?' during the addition.

media.context: Plays on M3.S4.T4.C44, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: On a parchment background, the title "Multiplying in Egyptian Numerals" fades in beside the hieroglyph symbols ∩, 9, 𝖠⁺, and 𝒞 drawn in a row. The video first animates landmark-times-ten products: ∩ × ∩ transforms into 9, then 9 × ∩ into 𝖠⁺, then 𝖠⁺ × ∩ into 𝒞, each shown with an Orange arrow and the caption "10ᵏ × 10 = 10ᵏ⁺¹". A pause card poses the textbook prompt "What is any landmark number multiplied by ∩ (10)?" with the four products (i)-(iv) listed and unanswered. The screen then builds Worked Example 1, "99 × ∩", line by line: 99 splits into 9 + 9, the distributive law spreads ∩ across both terms, and the result collapses to 𝖠⁺𝖠⁺. A second pause card shows the CHECK question about base-5 (5² × 5³ = 5⁵). Worked Example 2, "9∩∩| × ∩", is revealed step by step into 𝖠⁺99∩, followed by an ERROR ALERT caption warning that "add a zero" does not work in Egyptian. A final recap contrasts Egyptian landmarks with Roman numerals.
media.teaching_notes: WHEN to play: Use this after students have attempted the two EXPLORE prompts ("landmark × ∩" and "landmark × 9") on their own, then again during review of the distributive-law worked examples. PAUSE 1, at ~50s on the EXPLORE card ("What is any landmark number multiplied by ∩?"): freeze before the reasoning appears and have students compute (i)-(iv) in their notebooks; point to the rule '10ᵏ × 10 = 10ᵏ⁺¹' and ask why the power goes up by one (attempt-before-reveal). PAUSE 2, at ~85s, just after Worked Example 1 finishes with 𝖠⁺𝖠⁺ and before Worked Example 2 starts: point to '9∩∩|' and ask "Predict the next step, how do we split this three-term number and where does ∩ go?" Also pause at ~120s on the base-5 CHECK card ('5² × 5³ = 5⁵') and ask students to argue in one sentence why the property must hold for any base-n, and why V × L does NOT give another Roman landmark. Do not let the video reveal the base-5 answer, that is for them to justify.

[Style]: 2D animation, clean whiteboard/parchment style, step-by-step reveal; pure white or subtle parchment background; Lilly font; clean handwritten-style numerals and hieroglyph symbols. [Scene sequence]: Scene 1, Hook (0-22s): On parchment, title "Multiplying in Egyptian Numerals" appears with the symbols ∩, 9, 𝖠⁺, 𝒞 drawn in a row. Caption: "If two landmark numbers are both powers of the same base, their product is always another landmark number." Narrator poses the curiosity. Scene 2, Landmark × ∩ (22-55s): Animate ∩ × ∩ → 9, then 9 × ∩ → 𝖠⁺, then 𝖠⁺ × ∩ → 𝒞, each with an Orange transformation arrow and the on-screen rule '10ᵏ × 10 = 10ᵏ⁺¹'. Pause at 50s: a card shows 'EXPLORE: What is any landmark number multiplied by ∩ (10)?' listing (i) ∩ × ∩ (ii) 9 × ∩ (iii) 𝖠⁺ × ∩ (iv) 𝒞 × ∩, narrator asks "Pause and compute each product in your notebook before we reveal the reasoning." Scene 3, Worked Example 1 (55-90s): Reveal line by line, one step at a time: 'Step 1: 99 is the same as 9 + 9', 'Step 2: 99 × ∩ = (9 + 9) × ∩', 'Step 3: = 9 × ∩ + 9 × ∩ = 𝖠⁺ + 𝖠⁺ = 𝖠⁺𝖠⁺'. Answer 𝖠⁺𝖠⁺ ticked. Pause at 85s: narrator asks "What would you do to multiply 9∩∩| by ∩ next?" Scene 4, Worked Example 2 + base-n check (90-135s): Build '9∩∩| × ∩ = (9 + ∩∩ + |) × ∩ = (9 × ∩) + (∩∩ × ∩) + (| × ∩) = 𝖠⁺ + 99 + ∩ = 𝖠⁺99∩' step by step. Then a CHECK card: 'Does this hold in base-5? Try 5² × 5³ = 5⁵.', leave it posed, do not solve. Show an ERROR ALERT caption: "Egyptian has no 0, every symbol promotes to the next landmark, you do NOT just add a zero." Scene 5, Recap + bridge (135-165s): Two columns, Egyptian landmarks (Navy Blue) always producing another landmark vs Roman numerals (grey) that do not; closing caption "A number system with a base is efficient in arithmetic too." Bridge text "Our modern Hindu number system is built on this structure." [Narration style]: calm, instructional; use phrases like "Notice how every product is the next landmark" and "The key idea here is that each landmark is a power of 10." [Music]: none or very subtle. [Visual elements]: 5-colour palette, Navy Blue, Orange, pale yellow, grey, white. The varied/new result symbol in Orange, the stable starting landmark in Navy Blue; Orange arrows showing each multiplication transformation; pale-yellow highlight boxes around the final answers; clean handwritten-style numerals and hieroglyphs throughout.

topics.summary: Choosing landmark numbers to be the powers of one number gives a base. The Egyptian base ten and a base-five variant both bundle base-many of a landmark into the next, which makes writing and adding easy.

content.text: The Egyptians gave a separate symbol to each power of ten: a stroke for 1, an arch for 10, a coil for 100, a lotus for 1000, and so on. To write a number, you count how many of each landmark it contains, exactly the digits of the number. So 3402 is 3 lotus, 4 coil, no arch, and 2 stroke. To read a numeral, add each landmark's value times how many times it appears. No symbol is ever used ten or more times, because ten of one landmark bundle up into a single one of the next.

content.text: A number system is called base-n when its landmark numbers are the powers of n: 1, then n, then n times n, and so on, and whenever a place gathers n of a landmark they bundle up into one of the next. The Egyptian system is base ten. A base-5 system has landmarks 1, 5, 25, 125. To write a number in a base, count how many of each landmark it holds, taking as many of the biggest as you can and keeping every count below the base. Because n of a landmark make the next, no count ever reaches n.

content.text: When you add two numbers written with landmark powers, you first pile together the like landmarks: ones with ones, tens with tens. If any pile reaches the base, say ten, you bundle those ten up into one of the next landmark and pass it along. This passing along is the carry. So 6 ones plus 8 ones is 14, which is 1 ten carried and 4 ones left. In a base-5 system the same rule uses five instead of ten. A carry is nothing more than the rule that the base-many of one landmark equal one of the next.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what giving each power of ten its own symbol accomplishes through observation and reasoning, and determine that a number is written by counting how many of each landmark it holds, so three thousand four hundred two is three thousand-symbols, four hundred-symbols, no ten-symbols and two ones. They will explain that no landmark symbol ever appears ten or more times, because ten of any landmark bundle up into a single one of the next.

Students will be able to infer what makes a number system base-n through observation and reasoning, and determine that its landmarks are the powers of n, one then n then n times n, and that writing a number counts how many of each landmark it holds while keeping every count below n. They will explain that no count ever reaches n, because whenever a place gathers n of a landmark they bundle into one of the next.

Students will be able to infer what happens when two numbers written with landmark powers are added through observation and reasoning, and determine that like landmarks pile together and any pile reaching the base bundles into one of the next and passes along as a carry, so six ones plus eight ones is one ten carried and four ones left. They will explain that a carry is nothing more than the rule that base-many of one landmark equal one of the next.

media.title: Place Value Expander
media.context: CBSE Class 8, Ganita Prakash Ch.3 'A Story of Numbers', the section where positional notation is unpacked. The class has already built columns by bundling, so the columns exist and this tool reads out what they were always saying. It uses the chapter's own landmark-number register — the places are n to the 0, n, n squared, n cubed counted FROM THE RIGHT — and the Class 7 exponent notation the student already has, so 10 cubed, 10 to the 0 and 10 to the minus 1 are all legal here. No bundling is re-taught and no base other than ten is introduced; the base work belongs to the Base Builder and the placeholder work to the Zero Placeholder Breaker.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. overview.goal: The student writes a number in expanded form using powers of ten and distinguishes the value of a digit from its face value.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: Three stacked panels on a plain working ground, the number in coloured columns above the sum it comes apart into. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class reads the leading digit of a four digit number as being worth its face value, and the coloured columns are asked to say what that digit is really worth.
overview.concept: Every digit in a number carries a value made of two things: the digit itself and the place it sits in. The value of a digit is the digit multiplied by the power of ten for its column, so the 4 in 4072 is worth 4000 and not 4. Writing the number as the sum of these values is the expanded form, and it is the same number written a different way.
overview.purpose: The student writes a number in expanded form using powers of ten and distinguishes the value of a digit from its face value.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Panels stack down the main panel at both widths, with the columns aligned above their terms so the vertical link is readable. On a 390 px frame long numbers scroll the column row horizontally rather than shrinking the digits. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not fill the expansion while a prediction is still open, and never omit a zero term. An omitted zero term teaches exactly the error the next tool exists to break.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. A positional numeral is a shorthand for a sum. Each column was created by bundling, so a digit in the hundreds column stands for that many hundreds and nothing else. Recovering the sum is therefore not a new operation, it is reading the numeral out in full. The empty places matter for the same reason: a 0 term contributes nothing to the total but holds every other digit in its own column. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.
