teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to replace a ranking with a matching. Every card on the left is joined to the problem it DID answer, and the limitation it left is printed in the same breath — so 'primitive' has nowhere to live: achievement and limitation arrive on the same line, for every system on the board.

Beat 2 is the whole argument in one picture and it is drawn before a word is said. 61 and 3601 are written in base sixty as two wedge groups each, and on screen they are the same picture. The zero is then inserted into 3601 and the two writings separate. That is why position alone is not enough, and it is the beat that makes 'position already handles empty columns' fail on sight.

Beat 3 carries the rule to the case that looks different and obeys it. Positional notation and Mesopotamian base sixty both gained 'place decides value' and neither gained a placeholder, so the strip draws them on ONE rung. Say that the strip is scaled by property and not by date — a class reading it as a timeline will expect every system to have a rung of its own.
media.generation_prompt: Number System Timeline Matcher: systems on the left and the problem each one solved on the right, connected by drawn links, with a compact timeline strip appearing once the board is complete
media.instructions_for_student: The left column lists ways of writing numbers. The right column lists the problems they solved. Tap a system, then tap the problem it answered, and the link is drawn. Each system answers exactly one problem, so a second link from the same card is refused, and a wrong link fades away with the reason it did not hold. When every system is linked, order the chain by the property each one gained and the strip opens beneath. Two systems that gained the same property share a place — that is a real answer, not a mistake.

media.title: The Journey to Europe and the Naming of Numerals
media.context: Plays on M5.S6.T6.C73, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: The video opens on a parchment world map with the on-screen question "If our digits came from India, how did the whole planet end up using them?" A glowing set of digits 0-9 sits over India, then an animated arrow sweeps westwards across deserts and trade routes to the Arab world, where the captions "Al-Khwarizmi, On the Calculation with Hindu Numerals (c. 825)" and "Al-Kindi, On the Use of the Hindu Numerals (c. 830)" appear beside their books. A second arrow carries the numerals onward to Europe by 1100 CE, where Fibonacci (around 1200) is shown urging adoption while stubborn Roman numerals (XIV) sit in the way until the 17th-century Renaissance. A five-beat vertical timeline then builds checkpoint by checkpoint (c. 200 BCE, c. 499 CE, c. 825 CE, c. 1200 CE, c. 17th century CE), followed by a split panel comparing the labels "Arabic numerals," "Hindu numerals," and "Hindu-Arabic numerals," and a final strip animating the digit shapes evolving Brahmi to Dürer. The closing card poses the CHECK question on-screen.
media.teaching_notes: Play this after students have learned that the Bakhshali manuscript and Aryabhata recorded the Indian number system in India, as the next beat in the story. Pause at 22s on the world map and ask the class to predict the route the numerals took before the arrow moves, an attempt-before-reveal prompt ("Trace on paper which direction and which regions the digits travelled through next"). Pause again at 80s, just as the Navy Blue Roman numerals XIV block the path, and ask "Why did Europe hold on to Roman numerals for several more centuries instead of switching right away?" before the Renaissance clears them. At the 120-150s naming panel, point to the three labels and ask students to justify which usage best reflects the numerals' true origin. Hold on the final CHECK card (150-165s) and have students write their one-sentence answer before any discussion.

media.description: The video opens on a parchment background with the question "What was the very first reason humans needed to count?" then animates a Stone Age scene where simple tally marks count food, animals in livestock, and the passing days toward a new moon and full moon. A globe spins and an arrow lands on India as the caption "Origin: thousands of years ago in India" appears. The Yajurveda names then line up beside their powers of 10 in a vertical column: eka to 1, dasa to 10, shata to 100, sahasra to 1,000, ayuta to 10,000, each row revealed with an arrow labelled "x 10". Next a parchment scroll labelled "Bakhshali manuscript (c. 3rd century CE)" shows the digits 0 through 9 with 0 drawn as a dot, followed by a portrait card for "Aryabhata (c. 499 CE)". The final scene displays the on-screen question asking the viewer to name the text and the mathematician.
media.teaching_notes: Play this after students have met Reema's four questions and are beginning the first one (since when have humans counted). It can also be shown during review of the chapter's opening. Pause at 95s when the column ends at 'ayuta -> 10,000' and ask students to predict the value of the next name before continuing, this is the attempt-before-reveal moment; let them apply the 'multiply by 10' rule (expecting 100,000) rather than reading it off. Pause again at 100s on the scroll and point to the 0 drawn as a dot, asking 'Why was zero first written as a dot, and which manuscript shows it?' At the final screen (140-160s) pause on the question and have students name the text (Bakhshali manuscript) and the mathematician (Aryabhata) from memory before peeking back at the paragraph.

media.description: The video opens on a parchment scroll titled 'A Story of Numbers', with Stone Age tally marks on a bone fading into Hindu-Arabic digits on a calculator. A horizontal timeline animates the eight number systems studied, tally marks, body parts, Gumulgal pair-counting, Roman numerals, Egyptian hieroglyphs, Mesopotamian sexagesimal, Mayan, Chinese rod, and the Hindu system. A five-rung ladder labelled 'Evolution of Ideas in Number Representation' then builds upward, each rung revealing one great idea, a fixed standard sequence, landmark numbers, powers of a number as landmarks (base-n), position as value (place value), and 0 as both placeholder and number, with the matching system name written beside it in Orange. A side-by-side panel writes the number 375 in five systems: Hindu 375, Egyptian (three 100s, seven 10s, five 1s), Roman CCCLXXV, Mesopotamian (6) × 60 + 15, and Chinese rod (3) × 100 + (7) × 10 + 5. The closing scene poses the notebook ladder task on-screen and pauses.
media.teaching_notes: Play this AFTER students have attempted the CHECK task, having them first sketch the 'Evolution of Ideas in Number Representation' ladder from Topic 23 on their own, then use the video to confirm. Best used as a whole-chapter review session. Pause at 105s, after the five-rung ladder is complete, and point to each rung asking students to name from memory the system that first embodied that idea before the Orange labels are read aloud (attempt-before-reveal). Pause again at 145s on the side-by-side '375' panel and ask 'Why does the Hindu writing need the fewest symbols?' to surface the role of 0 and place value. Closing question to pose: 'Trap 1 says older systems were useless, why is that wrong?' to push students to explain that each got us one step closer.
media.generation_prompt: [Duration]: 170 seconds. [Style]: 2D animation, clean whiteboard/parchment style, step-by-step reveal; pure white or subtle parchment background; Lilly font; clean handwritten-style numerals and symbols. [Scene sequence]: Scene 1 Hook (0-25s): A bone with tally marks morphs into Hindu-Arabic digits on a calculator. On-screen caption 'A Story of Numbers' then 'What did every civilisation actually contribute?'. Narrator poses the journey from Stone Age tally marks to today's digits. Scene 2 Recall the eight systems (25-55s): A timeline draws left to right, dropping in labels one by one, 'tally marks', 'body parts', 'Gumulgal', 'Roman', 'Egyptian', 'Mesopotamian', 'Mayan', 'Chinese rod', 'Hindu'. Caption 'Every one contributed at least one of five great ideas.' Scene 3 The ladder of five ideas (55-105s): A five-rung ladder titled 'Evolution of Ideas in Number Representation' builds upward. Each rung writes one idea and its system in Orange: 'A fixed standard sequence -> body-part system', 'Landmark numbers -> Roman', 'Powers of a number as landmarks (base-n) -> Egyptian', 'Position as value (place value) -> Mesopotamian, Mayan, Chinese', '0 as digit AND number -> Hindu'. Scene 4 The number 375 in five systems (105-150s): A side panel writes 'Hindu: 375', 'Egyptian: three 100s, seven 10s, five 1s', 'Roman: CCCLXXV', 'Mesopotamian: (6) × 60 + 15', 'Chinese rod: (3) × 100 + (7) × 10 + 5'. Caption 'All five name the same quantity, 375.' Pause at 145s: narrator asks 'Which writing looks the most efficient to you?' Scene 5 Recap + check task (150-170s): The ladder reappears with caption 'CHECK: draw the ladder and name one system that first embodied each idea.' Narrator gives the bridge that the Hindu system packages all five ideas in the simplest way. [Narration style]: calm, instructional; use phrases like 'Notice how each system added one step' and 'The key idea here is that no system invented itself from scratch'. [Music]: none or very subtle. [Visual elements]: 5-colour palette (Navy Blue, Orange, pale yellow, grey, white); the new idea on each ladder rung and the system that first embodied it shown in Orange, the stable summary structure in Navy Blue; arrows showing the transformation from one idea to the next; clean handwritten-style numerals and the actual symbols CCCLXXV and the base-60 grouping.
media.instructions_for_student: Watch the animation on Summary, The Five Great Ideas in the Evolution of Number Systems, then be ready to explain it in your own words.

content.text: The same positional numeral can be read aloud in two ways. The Indian system groups the digits 3, then 2, then 2 from the right, so the names land on thousand, lakh and crore. The international system groups them 3, 3, 3, so the names land on thousand, million and billion. The commas are only a reading aid: the digit string is identical under both, which is why one crore and ten million are the same number written the same way and read differently.

objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what pairing the members of two collections one to one reveals through observation and reasoning, and determine that when both sides run out together the collections are equal, while any objects left over mark the larger side and count exactly how many more the smaller side needs. They will explain that this comparison names which collection is bigger and by how much without any counting words or digits at all.

Students will be able to infer what a fixed-order standard sequence does for counting through observation and reasoning, and determine that the symbol a count stops on is its name, so a sequence of only twenty-six letters can name no collection larger than twenty-six. They will explain that a usable number system must be an unending sequence, since a finite set of symbols eventually runs out and leaves large collections with no name.
Examine the worked examples of a number system as a fixed-order standard sequence, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving a number system as a fixed-order standard sequence, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer what bundling single tally marks into equal groups achieves through observation and reasoning, and determine that the total is the group size times the number of full bundles plus the leftover marks, so four groups of five and three over is twenty-three. They will explain that a grouped tally is read far faster than one plain mark per object, which is exactly why people began bundling their marks.

Students will be able to infer what a system built on pairs records through observation and reasoning, and determine that each pair-word stands for two and a single unit-word for a leftover one, so a string of three pair-words with one unit is seven. They will explain that reading such a name means counting two for every pair-word and one for the leftover, and that grouping in twos is already shorter to write than a plain tally.

Students will be able to infer what a set of landmark symbols does for writing numbers through observation and reasoning, and determine that a number is built by taking landmarks from largest to smallest, with a smaller symbol before a larger one meaning one landmark less, so four is IV and ninety is XC. They will explain that reading adds the symbols while subtracting whenever a smaller one sits before a larger one, letting a few landmarks stand for large numbers far more compactly than a tally.

Students will be able to infer what giving each power of ten its own symbol accomplishes through observation and reasoning, and determine that a number is written by counting how many of each landmark it holds, so three thousand four hundred two is three thousand-symbols, four hundred-symbols, no ten-symbols and two ones. They will explain that no landmark symbol ever appears ten or more times, because ten of any landmark bundle up into a single one of the next.

Students will be able to infer what makes a number system base-n through observation and reasoning, and determine that its landmarks are the powers of n, one then n then n times n, and that writing a number counts how many of each landmark it holds while keeping every count below n. They will explain that no count ever reaches n, because whenever a place gathers n of a landmark they bundle into one of the next.
Examine the worked examples of the idea of a base, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving the idea of a base, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer what happens when two numbers written with landmark powers are added through observation and reasoning, and determine that like landmarks pile together and any pile reaching the base bundles into one of the next and passes along as a carry, so six ones plus eight ones is one ten carried and four ones left. They will explain that a carry is nothing more than the rule that base-many of one landmark equal one of the next.

objectives.strand_name: Place value and the invention of zero
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what tells a digit its value in a positional system through observation and reasoning, and determine that each column carries a landmark, the ones, the sixties, the three thousand six hundreds, so a two in the sixties column is worth one hundred twenty and the whole numeral is the sum of digit times landmark. They will explain that moving a digit one column to the left multiplies its value by the base.

objectives.strand_name: Place value and the invention of zero
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what goes wrong when a positional column is left blank through observation and reasoning, and determine that a blank cannot say how many columns are empty, so the same marks could be read as several different numbers such as sixty-one, three thousand six hundred one, or three thousand six hundred sixty. They will explain that a written zero names each empty column exactly and gives a numeral one single reading, which is why zero was invented as a placeholder.

objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what converting a number between an early positional system and our numerals really requires through observation and reasoning, and determine that reading a numeral sums each digit times its landmark while writing one peels off the largest landmark first, so four sixties and ten ones is two hundred fifty. They will explain that conversion is exactly the sum of digit times landmark that a positional numeral already stands for, with a written zero keeping every step unambiguous.

how_to_use.intro: This is the story of how humans learned to write numbers, rebuilt idea by idea. Each section pairs a short, plain explanation with one interactive tool, and every old number system is something you reconstruct by hand rather than just read about.

points.text: Each idea, matching, grouping, choosing a base, using position and a zero, is explored by hand before it is practised.
points.title: One tool per section

points.text: Worked examples are demonstrated in Learn mode, then the same skill is practised in Play mode where answers turn green or red.
points.title: Learn then Play

points.text: Every tool asks you to commit a guess before it shows the answer, so you discover the idea instead of being told it.
points.title: Predict, then reveal, then explain why

points.text: Videos carry the human story and artefacts a tool cannot show, and they always play after you have used the tool, never before.
points.title: Video after the tool

summary_stats.counts_note: One distinct tool per concept; each tool runs four mods (AI demo, Learn, Practice, Free Play), with one objective each for AI demo, Learn and Practice and none for Free Play.
summary_stats.videos_note: One 30 to 40 second curiosity hook video per topic, plus a chapter intro video and a chapter summary video of 1 to 2 minutes each.
summary_stats.tool_needed_note: Per-item boolean for how the ANSWER is entered, NOT whether to show the tool. The frontend ALWAYS renders the tool. true = the answer must be produced through the tool. false = the student reasons it out (typed/spoken) and the tool stays on screen as an aid.
summary_stats.solved_examples_note: Each solved example carries a first-person 'reasoning' field that generalises the method.
summary_stats.practice_problems_note: 154 practice items in all = (11 microconcepts x 10 tool-answered) + (11 x 4 reasoning items).
summary_stats.question_repository_note: Worked-example and practice questions are no longer inline. Each learn/practice concept carries a question_bank_ref into question_repository.json; the teacher agent pulls questions from the repository at teach time. The teaching (AI-demo) concept keeps its inline source_ai_reasoning block.

authoring_rules.nesting: Each objective contains exactly one concept; each concept contains its solved examples then its practice questions.
authoring_rules.solved_examples: At least 10 per microconcept; each is demonstrated on that section's tool with numbered steps, a final answer and first-person reasoning that models how to think, not just which buttons to press.
authoring_rules.practice_questions: At least 10 tool-answered items per microconcept (marked right/wrong on the tool), followed by exactly 4 reasoning items: application, reverse, explain, error_spotting.

mods.does: The AI teaches the whole concept and works the higher-order reasoning questions (application, reverse, explain, error-spotting) with full step-by-step explanations, with the tool on screen; the student only watches.
The AI demonstrates the worked examples one step at a time on the tool.
The student answers the tool-answered practice questions that reinforce the worked examples.
The student freely solves any question of the same kind on the tool, neither taught nor scored.

tool_mods_legend.note: Every tool runs four mods. Teach mods are AI operated; practice and play are student operated.
